title: Episode 4 of 5 · Midwest · 12 states
edition: Five videos · 48 contiguous states · John · November 2026
intro: Welcome to episode four of our U.S. states series. First, I clear the map so we can study a fresh group.
Today we explore all twelve Midwest states, from the Great Lakes through the Mississippi Valley to the central Plains. Lakes, river borders and north-south pairs will guide us.

states.name: Ohio
lines: Ohio sits immediately west of Pennsylvania, above Kentucky. Its northern edge reaches Lake Erie; the Ohio River curves along much of its southern border.
The name comes from a Seneca expression for a good or great river. The Wright brothers developed their aircraft in Dayton, before flying in North Carolina.
Use Ohio as our eastern gateway to the Midwest. Indiana lies to its west, while Michigan reaches down from the north.
states.transition: Let's begin with Ohio on Lake Erie, then travel around the Great Lakes and west across the Midwest.

states.name: Michigan
states.transition: We'll widen the view northward for Michigan. Its two main peninsulas need to be seen together, across the Great Lakes.
lines: Michigan has a mitten-shaped Lower Peninsula and a separate Upper Peninsula extending west above Lake Michigan. Both belong to the same state.
Its name refers to large water. The Mackinac Bridge connects the two peninsulas across the Straits of Mackinac; it opened in 1957.
Do not mistake the Upper Peninsula for Wisconsin. Michigan's two parts frame the northern end of Lake Michigan, while Indiana is farther south.

states.name: Indiana
states.transition: Now follow Lake Michigan south. We'll study Indiana and Illinois side by side before continuing up the lake's western shore.
lines: Indiana lies west of Ohio and east of Illinois, with Kentucky below it. Its short northern shoreline touches Lake Michigan.
The name means land of the Indians, a name given by settlers. The first Indianapolis 500 motor race was held here in 1911.
Remember Indiana as the middle state in this east-west sequence: Ohio, Indiana, Illinois. We move one state west next.

states.name: Illinois
lines: Illinois is the long state west of Indiana. Chicago sits in its northeastern corner on Lake Michigan, while the Mississippi River forms its western edge.
Its name comes through French from the Illinois peoples, and the final s is silent. Chicago rebuilt after its 1871 fire and became a centre of early skyscraper design.
Keep Illinois between Indiana and the Mississippi. Wisconsin lies directly above it, along the western side of Lake Michigan.

states.name: Wisconsin
states.transition: Let's move north and west to Wisconsin and Minnesota. The Great Lakes give way to the upper Mississippi and a landscape of many smaller lakes.
lines: Wisconsin lies north of Illinois, between Minnesota and Lake Michigan. Lake Superior touches its northern edge, below Michigan's Upper Peninsula.
The card highlights Wisconsin's cheese-making identity. Dairy farming and cheese production are central to the state's America’s Dairyland nickname.
Remember Wisconsin on Lake Michigan's western shore. Minnesota is immediately to the west, across river borders in the south and on land farther north.

states.name: Minnesota
lines: Minnesota is west of Wisconsin and north of Iowa. Its northeastern tip reaches Lake Superior, and its northern boundary meets Canada.
Its Dakota-derived name is associated with sky-tinted or cloudy water. The Mississippi River begins here at Lake Itasca, far from its mouth in Louisiana.
Keep Minnesota above Iowa and east of the Dakotas. Our next move follows the Mississippi south, toward Iowa and Missouri.

states.name: Iowa
states.transition: We now move south along the Mississippi Valley. Iowa and Missouri form another useful north-south pair.
lines: Iowa lies directly below Minnesota, with the Mississippi along its eastern edge. Nebraska is to its west and Missouri below it.
The name comes from the Ioway people. The card points to Iowa's farming identity; corn production is a major part of the state's agriculture.
Remember Iowa between the Missouri River on the west and the Mississippi on the east. Missouri, our next state, is directly south.

states.name: Missouri
lines: Missouri sits below Iowa and west of Illinois. The Mississippi forms its eastern boundary; the Missouri River crosses the state toward St Louis.
The card connects Missouri with westward travel. In St Louis, the Gateway Arch commemorates the city's role in the westward expansion of the United States.
Look for Missouri's small southeastern bootheel. Kansas lies to the west; we now turn toward the central Plains.

states.name: Kansas
states.transition: Let's frame Kansas and Nebraska, two broad Plains states stacked north and south. Then we'll continue north through the Dakotas.
lines: Kansas lies west of Missouri, directly above Oklahoma and below Nebraska. Most of its outline is rectangular, apart from its northeastern river boundary.
Its name comes from the Kansa people. The Topeka case in Brown versus Board of Education helped lead to the 1954 ruling that racial segregation in public schools was unconstitutional.
Remember Kansas above Oklahoma and below Nebraska. Unlike Arkansas, its final s is pronounced; those are two different states.

states.name: Nebraska
lines: Nebraska stretches across the Plains above Kansas. Notice the notch in its southwestern corner and the Missouri River along its eastern side.
Its name refers to flat water, linked to the Platte River. Nebraska has the country's only one-house state legislature, officially organised on a nonpartisan basis.
Think of Nebraska as the next rung north from Kansas. South Dakota lies above it; Iowa is across the Missouri River to the east.

states.name: South Dakota
states.transition: Our final close view takes in both Dakotas, from Nebraska's northern border up to Canada. Watch the two stacked outlines.
lines: South Dakota lies above Nebraska and below North Dakota. Minnesota is to the east, while the Black Hills are in the western part of the state.
The card recalls Mount Rushmore, carved between 1927 and 1941 in the Black Hills. The area is sacred to the Lakota, and its history remains contested.
Remember South Dakota as the lower Dakota. Its northern neighbour shares both its name and the day it became a state.

states.name: North Dakota
lines: North Dakota is directly above South Dakota, along the Canadian border. Minnesota is to its east and Montana to its west.
Dakota means friend or ally. Both Dakotas joined the Union on November second, 1889; the signing papers were shuffled so the order was not recorded.
North Dakota completes our twelve Midwest states. Trace the Plains stack from south to north: Kansas, Nebraska, South Dakota, North Dakota.

recap: Start with Ohio, Michigan, Indiana and Illinois; continue around the lakes to Wisconsin and Minnesota. Then locate Iowa above Missouri.
Finish with the Plains stack: Kansas, Nebraska, South Dakota and North Dakota. That completes all twelve Midwest states. One final episode will take us across the West.
